Here is the full corrected final answer:

---

## The single condition

The rig's root btrfs filesystem remounted **read-only** due to metadata corruption on the marginal OS NVMe (WD SN570 2TB, serial `210318800752`, PCIe `0000:74:00.0`). The NVMe has a known marginal PCIe link — a metadata write is corrupted in flight (bad data written under a *valid* checksum, so `btrfs device stats` shows **0** corruption errors). btrfs detects the stale/torn leaf (parent transid verify fail: parent points at generation 16495 but the leaf on disk still holds 16087), sets the fs error state, and refuses to remount rw (`remounting read-write after error is not allowed`).

Every symptom maps directly:

| Symptom | Why it happens |
|---|---|
| `restic-backup`, `ansible-pull`, `logrotate` all fail | They can't write anything to a ro filesystem |
| Palworld flips unhealthy, REST port dead | Can't write game saves to the overlay |
| LiteLLM returns `503 no_db_connection` | Postgres (`litellm-db`) segfaulted (exit 139) on a failed WAL write |
| `/health/liveliness` still 200 | Master-key liveness check doesn't hit the DB — only virtual-key clients do |
| `docker ps` shows everything `Up (healthy)` | The daemon can't persist state to the read-only disk; it reports stale health |

---

## Confirm it in one command

```bash
ssh rig 'findmnt -no OPTIONS / | cut -d, -f1'
```

If it returns **`ro`**, you're in this incident. The verification check `rig-root-fs-writable` does the same thing (plus a real `touch` probe). A secondary probe:

```bash
ssh rig 'touch /home/btabaska/.probe && rm /home/btabaska/.probe && echo RW || echo RO'
```

---

## Why a plain reboot won't fix it

The NVMe's marginal PCIe link causes the *same* corruption on every boot. btrfs re-hits the bad leaf on mount, refuses the rw transition, and the machine boots into **emergency mode** with root mounted read-only. A reboot cycles through the exact same failure path — it doesn't heal the link or repair the filesystem.

---

## Documented recovery order

From `rig-btrfs-readonly-recovery.md` (first occurrence 2026-07-15, task `fix-20`):

### 1. Salvage un-backed-up deltas (while the fs is still readable `ro`)

```bash
# on mini: receive
tmux new -d -s salvage 'nc -lvnp 9998 > ~/rig-salvage/rig-salvage.tar.gz'

# on rig (root): send worlds/saves + docker volumes + /etc
cd / && tar czf - --ignore-failed-read \
  --exclude='*.jar' --exclude='*/libraries' --exclude='*/versions' --exclude='*/steamapps' \
  opt/stacks/palworld/game/Pal/Saved opt/stacks/palworld/game/backups \
  opt/stacks/amp/config/.ampdata var/lib/docker/volumes/docker_litellm_pgdata \
  var/lib/docker/volumes/docker_open_webui_data etc | socat -u - TCP:192.168.10.2:9998

# verify on mini: gzip -t rig-salvage.tar.gz && tar tzf rig-salvage.tar.gz | wc -l
```

### 2. Reseat the marginal NVMe (heals the link before repair writes)

Power off (hold the power button — `systemctl` loops back to emergency mode). Reseat the WD 2TB NVMe, ideally into a **different M.2 slot** to rule out the slot. This is the durable fix for the *cause*; the btrfs repair only fixes the *damage*.

### 3. Offline btrfs repair from a Linux USB

Boot any Linux live USB with `btrfs-progs`. Select the fs **by UUID** (the `nvmeN` number changes across reboots/reseats):

```bash
UUID=e4b84b06-355f-4d67-8d41-05a152472392    # the rig root btrfs (partition …p2)
umount /dev/disk/by-uuid/$UUID 2>/dev/null
btrfs check --readonly /dev/disk/by-uuid/$UUID | tee /tmp/pre.txt     # assess (expect the transid error)
btrfs check --repair   /dev/disk/by-uuid/$UUID | tee /tmp/repair.txt  # fix
btrfs check --readonly /dev/disk/by-uuid/$UUID | tee /tmp/post.txt    # MUST be clean
```

- **`post.txt` clean** → remove USB, boot into CachyOS (root now mounts **rw**), go to step 4.
- **`--repair` cannot fix it** → do **not** loop `--repair`. Restore from the last pre-corruption restic snapshot / reinstall (you have the step-1 salvage). See `backup-restore.md`.

### 4. Bring services back and re-verify (consumer-level, not liveness)

```bash
ssh rig 'findmnt -no OPTIONS / | cut -d, -f1'            # expect: rw
ssh rig 'sudo systemctl start docker && docker compose --project-directory /opt/stacks/palworld up -d'
# litellm-db segfaulted mid-write — check Postgres came up clean; restore the volume from salvage if not
ssh rig 'docker inspect -f "{{.State.Running}} {{.State.ExitCode}}" litellm-db palworld'
ssh rig 'sudo systemctl start restic-backup.service'     # closes the backup gap (H23/H27)
```

Then confirm the fix-20 checks are green: `rig-root-fs-writable`, `rig-litellm-vkey-e2e`, `systemd-failed-rig`, `containers-manifest-rig`, `palworld-rest-liveness`, `restic-snapshot-fresh-rig`.

---

## Standing hardware note

The marginal PCIe link is the recurring cause. Reseating addresses it short-term; **replace the SN570** (serial `210318800752`) if corruption recurs after a reseat. Tracked in memory `rig-nvme-pcie-link`.

## House DNS Design — Full Walkthrough

### The resolver chain handed out by DHCP (every client VLAN)

Three resolvers, in strict priority order:

| # | IP | Host / Service | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | `192.168.10.2` | Mac mini — AdGuard Home | **Primary** filtering + `*.tabaska.us` DNS rewrites. Forwards external lookups to **Unbound** (local recursive resolver with DNSSEC) on `127.0.0.1:5335`. |
| **2** | `192.168.10.4` | NAS (DS920+) — AdGuard Home | **Secondary** filtering + mirrors the `*.tabaska.us → 192.168.10.2` rewrites. Forwards external lookups to **public DoT** (`tls://1.1.1.1`, `tls://9.9.9.9`) — *not* mini Unbound, so it works independently. |
| **3** | `192.168.10.1` | UniFi gateway | **Survival fallback** — bare internet DNS, no filtering, no local rewrites. |

Both AdGuard instances rewrite every `*.tabaska.us` query to `192.168.10.2`.

### Upstream for each hop

```
mini AdGuard (192.168.10.2)
  └── Unbound (127.0.0.1:5335) → recursive, DNSSEC → root/TLD servers

NAS AdGuard (192.168.10.4)
  └── Public DoT (tls://1.1.1.1 / tls://9.9.9.9) → Cloudflare/Quad9 resolvers

UniFi gateway (192.168.10.1)
  └── ISP's DNS (bare internet)
```

### Why `*.tabaska.us` looks dead when the mini is down — even though DNS "succeeds"

This is the key behavioral quirk, documented in both the outage runbook and the resilience design doc:

**What the user sees:** WiFi connected, internet works (Google loads), but `wiki.tabaska.us`, `home.tabaska.us`, every `*.tabaska.us` site is unreachable.

**What's actually happening:**

1. The client's DHCP lease hands it `{192.168.10.2, 192.168.10.4, 192.168.10.1}` as DNS servers.
2. When the mini goes down, the client tries `192.168.10.2` (mini AdGuard) — it doesn't answer.
3. The client falls to **hop 2** — NAS AdGuard (`192.168.10.4`), which *is* running.
4. NAS AdGuard has the **same `*.tabaska.us → 192.168.10.2` rewrites**, so it returns `192.168.10.2` as the answer. DNS resolution **succeeds** — the client gets an IP address back.
5. But `192.168.10.2` is the mini's IP, and the mini is down. Caddy (the web proxy) is not listening. The HTTP connection to `wiki.tabaska.us` connects to an unreachable host.

**In short:** DNS resolution works (the NAS rewrite delivers the right IP), but the *service* at that IP is offline. The user's browser says "site can't be reached" even though `dig` would show a valid answer.

**Verification from any LAN machine:**
```bash
# Hop 1 — mini AdGuard (dead when mini is down)
dig @192.168.10.2 wiki.tabaska.us +short        # expect 192.168.10.2 (or timeout)

# Hop 2 — NAS AdGuard (still answers the rewrite)
dig @192.168.10.4 wiki.tabaska.us +short        # still returns 192.168.10.2
dig @192.168.10.4 example.com +time=2 +tries=1  # external still resolves

# Direct port access still works (bypasses Caddy on mini entirely)
# e.g., 192.168.10.4:2283 (Immich), Plex, DSM, HA :8123
```

### Failure-mode summary

| What dies | Client behavior |
|---|---|
| **Mini reboot** (~30–60 s) | Clients retry → NAS AdGuard → internet + local names keep working |
| **Mini + NAS both down** | Clients retry → gateway DNS → **public internet works**; filtering + `*.tabaska.us` are lost until an AdGuard returns |
| **Gateway down** | Bigger problem — nothing in this design fixes that |

### Current state (validated 2026-07-14)

- ✅ **dns-01** — mini AdGuard + Unbound + rewrites: done
- ✅ **dns-02** — NAS AdGuard secondary (`adguard/adguardhome:v0.107.77`, port 53, break-glass admin at `http://192.168.10.4:3000`) + mirrored rewrites/blocklists: done
- ⚠️ **dns-03** — UniFi DHCP fail-open chain on all VLANs: **open** (requires manual UniFi GUI work — Settings → Networks → each VLAN → DHCP → DNS Server = `192.168.10.2, 192.168.10.4, 192.168.10.1`)
- ✅ **dns-04** — Verify script (`scripts/network/dns-resilience-verify.sh`) + outage runbook: done
- ⏳ **dns-05** — NAT `:53` redirect + DoH blocking: **deferred** (must not enable until dns-03 is live, or it recreates the single-point-of-failure)

### Verification checks

Six checks (`checks.d/dns.yaml`) run hourly/daily via the verification harness, paged via ntfy:

- `dns-mini-internal` — AdGuard (mini) resolves `home.tabaska.us` → expects `192.168.10.x`
- `dns-mini-external` — AdGuard (mini) resolves `example.com`
- `dns-mini-unbound-upstream` — Unbound on mini (`127.0.0.1:5335`) answers directly
- `dns-nas-internal` — NAS AdGuard (`192.168.10.4`) resolves `home.tabaska.us`
- `dns-nas-external` — NAS AdGuard resolves `example.com`
- `mini-container-dns-egress` — mini containers resolve external names via Docker DNS

The 2026-07-07 audit found off-subnet `192.168.1.1` in the DHCP handout; this was corrected to the proper chain.

**One claim to correct:**

> "So you can't `prune` away data within 30 days of its creation, but the mechanism doesn't break — it just defers the hard delete."

The kb does **not** say you can't prune within 30 days. It says restic ≥ 0.19 hides objects (which works under GOVERNANCE), and the lifecycle rule handles eventual hard delete after both the hide window and retention have passed. Restic *can* still run forget/prune — hiding is the mechanism, not a blockage. My phrasing implied a blockage that isn't in the evidence.

Here is the corrected full answer:

---

## Two B2 Buckets, Two Policies

| Bucket | Purpose | Retention-locked? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`bucket-restic`** | Restic repos from **mini** and **rig** (configs, dotfiles, game saves, etc.) | **Yes — GOVERNANCE 30-day default retention** | This is your immutable/ransomware-proof tier (the "1" in 3-2-1-1-0) |
| **`bucket-hyper-backup`** | NAS Hyper Backup task ("S3 Backup enc" → `TabaskaNAS_2.hbk`) | **No — deliberately NOT locked** (M37, accepted) | Hyper Backup's **Smart Recycle** rotation must be able to delete old versions; retention would break it |

### How `bucket-restic` is locked

- **Default retention:** GOVERNANCE mode, 30 days. Every object gets a 30-day retention window on upload.
- **One-time backfill:** On 2026-07-17, all 1,174 pre-existing pack versions were backfilled with the same retention.
- **Upload-time lock:** New uploads are locked automatically — the append-only keys on mini/rig need no extra capabilities.
- **Lifecycle rule:** `daysFromHidingToDeleting: 30`. This means hidden objects are hard-deleted 30 days after being hidden, but only after the retention window has also passed.

### How restic `forget`/`prune` works under the lock

Restic ≥ 0.19 handles deletion by **hiding** objects rather than hard-deleting them. Under B2 Object Lock GOVERNANCE mode:

1. `restic forget` + `restic prune` **hide** the snapshot pack files (they become invisible to restic but still exist on B2). Hiding is compatible with GOVERNANCE mode.
2. The B2 lifecycle rule (`daysFromHidingToDeleting: 30`) then **hard-deletes** them — but *only after* both the hide window and the 30-day retention have elapsed.

The mechanism doesn't break: restic can still run forget/prune normally (it hides), and the lifecycle rule handles the eventual hard delete.

### Why `bucket-hyper-backup` is intentionally NOT locked

Synology Hyper Backup's **Smart Recycle** rotation policy must be able to delete old backup versions to manage disk usage. Object Lock would prevent that entirely. The compensating controls are:

- The backup content is **client-side encrypted** (`enable_data_encrypt=true`), so even if someone reads or deletes objects, they're useless without the key (stored in vault `hosts.nas.hyperbackup_password` + Proton Pass).
- The delete-capable B2 master key is **retired from the vault** (see below).

### What happened to the B2 master application key

The B2 master key carries `deleteFiles` + `bypassGovernance` capabilities. That meant a laptop compromise or vault breach could **hard-delete everything** in `bucket-restic` despite the GOVERNANCE lock — the master key can override it.

**Resolution (fix-22):**

- The master key was **retired from the vault**. It now lives **offline** and is used only for bucket administration via `scripts/backup/b2-apply-bucket-policy.py` (idempotent re-apply + backfill).
- Day-to-day operations use the scoped **`b2-ops` key** (vault `backblaze_b2.ops_key_id` / `ops_key`) — this key has **list/read only** permissions. It cannot delete or modify objects.
- The append-only keys (`backblaze_b2.restic_append_only_key_id` / `_key`) used by restic on mini/rig remain in use — they are seeded into each host's `/etc/restic/env` and are sufficient for backup operations (append-only, no delete capability).

### Daily verification

Two checks in `verification/checks.d/backups.yaml` (task `fix-22`) confirm the design holds:

1. **`b2-restic-immutable`** (critical) — asserts the retention config is set **and** live-attempts a delete with the vault key, expecting HTTP 401 (forbidden).
2. **`b2-bucket-policy`** — validates the bucket-set manifest, catching unknown/typo buckets and policy drift.

### Context: how this got here

The quality-gate audit (H20) found that `bucket-restic` had File Lock *enabled* but **no default retention** and no per-file retention — the only guard was the append-only key. The fix (2026-07-17) added the GOVERNANCE 30-day default retention, backfilled existing objects, retired the master key from the vault, and added the daily verification checks.

## Immich Postgres Restore — Full Procedure

### Pre-flight

1. **SSH to the NAS and identify the dump to restore from.** The nightly pg_dump lands in `/volume1/docker/immich/backups/` at 02:30 (DSM Task Scheduler task 9), rotated to keep the 7 most recent (7-day window). Pick the one from just *before* the incident:

```bash
ssh nas
ls -lt /volume1/docker/immich/backups/
```

2. **Read the credentials** from the `.env` (never committed):

```bash
cat /volume1/docker/immich/.env
# Note: DB_USERNAME, DB_DATABASE_NAME, DB_PASSWORD
```

### Step 1 — Stop the app containers (keep Postgres up)

```bash
cd /volume1/docker/immich
sudo docker compose stop immich-server immich-machine-learning
```

> **Do NOT stop the Postgres container** — you need it running to accept the restore stream.

### Step 2 — Pick the dump

```bash
ls -lt /volume1/docker/immich/backups/
```

### Step 3 — Restore into the running Postgres container

```bash
gunzip -c /volume1/docker/immich/backups/<dump>.sql.gz \
  | sudo docker exec -i immich_postgres psql -U <DB_USERNAME> -d <DB_DATABASE_NAME>
```

For example:

```bash
gunzip -c /volume1/docker/immich/backups/immich-2026-08-14.sql.gz \
  | sudo docker exec -i immich_postgres psql -U <DB_USERNAME> -d <DB_DATABASE_NAME>
```

### Step 4 — Restart the app

```bash
sudo docker compose up -d
```

### Step 5 — Verify

```bash
# 1. Server responds
curl -fsS http://192.168.10.4:2283/api/server/ping
# Expected: {"res":"pong"}

# 2. Log in to https://immich.tabaska.us and spot-check:
#    - Albums are intact
#    - People/faces are correct
#    - Asset count matches expectations
```

### Important notes

- **Photo files on disk are NOT touched** during a DB restore — originals at `/volume1/photo` remain exactly where they are. Only the metadata (albums, faces, tags, DB-side records) is replaced.
- **The dump script** is `/volume1/scripts/nas/immich-db-dump.sh` (deployed from `foss-setup/scripts/nas/immich-db-dump.sh`), run by DSM Task Scheduler at 02:30 nightly. It produces gzipped SQL dumps to `/volume1/docker/immich/backups/` with a `KEEP_DAYS=7` rotation.
- **Postgres image is digest-pinned** (`ghcr.io/immich-app/postgres:14-vectorchord0.4.3-pgvectors0.2.0@sha256:bcf63357191b76a916ae5eb93464d65c07511da41e3bf7a8416db519b40b1c23`) — do not float the DB image.
- **The `.env` file** at `/volume1/docker/immich/.env` holds `DB_USERNAME`, `DB_DATABASE_NAME`, and `DB_PASSWORD` sourced from the vault (never committed). Use those values in the `psql` command.
- **Version bump safety:** Postgres major upgrades are not automatic. If the dump predates a Postgres major version change, a simple `.sql.gz` restore may fail — you'd need a proper cross-version migration. The fleet is on Postgres 14 (VectorChord) consistently, so this is an edge case.

input: I added a new vhost to the Caddyfile on the mini (and mirrored it into the repo), but browsers get a TLS 'internal error' for the new name while every other *.tabaska.us site works fine. The backend itself is up. What's the documented failure mode here, the exact fix, and the verification check that exists for precisely this?
reference: Failure mode: the Caddyfile was edited but caddy was never RELOADED — the RUNNING config, not the file on disk, serves traffic, so the running instance has no route or cert for the new vhost and clients get a TLS internal error (exactly the llamaswap incident, which ran 3 days). Standing rule: every Caddyfile edit must end with a reload — edit-without-reload is an incomplete change — and the edit must be mirrored to the repo Caddyfile plus the /opt/stacks git repo. Related context: the LAN wildcard *.tabaska.us -> 192.168.10.2 makes ANY unknown name resolve to caddy and fail the TLS handshake, which is normal for retired names, not an incident.

**`mini-caddy-live-config-current`** — added by **fix-32** (2026-07-18) specifically to prevent this class of incident. It:

1. Adapts the on-disk Caddyfile (`/opt/stacks/caddy/caddy/Caddyfile` inside the container) via `caddy adapt`
2. Fetches the live admin-API config from `http://localhost:2019/config/`
3. Extracts the host sets from both and diffs them

The check command (from `kb/wiki/reference/checks/mini-services.md` line 24):

```bash
{ docker exec caddy caddy adapt --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile 2>/dev/null; echo __SPLIT__; docker exec caddy wget -qO- http://localhost:2019/config/; } | python3 -c "import sys,json; raw=sys.stdin.read().split('__SPLIT__'); hosts=lambda c: {h for s in c.get('apps',{}).get('http',{}).get('servers',{}).values() for r in s.get('routes',[]) for m in r.get('match',[]) for h in m.get('host',[])}; disk=hosts(json.loads(raw[0])); live=hosts(json.loads(raw[1])); print('caddy_config=current' if disk==live else 'caddy_config=DRIFT missing_live:%s extra_live:%s' % (sorted(disk-live), sorted(live-disk)))"
```

- `missing_live:` = vhosts on disk that Caddy is not serving (the edit-without-reload case)
- `extra_live:` = vhosts removed from disk but still being served

If the adapted (disk) hosts don't match the live admin-API hosts, the check fails with the `caddy_config=DRIFT` message.

## The golden rule

From the same runbook: **"Every Caddyfile edit must end with a reload"** — treat edit-without-reload as an incomplete change, and mirror the edit to both `foss-setup/configs/docker-stack/stacks/caddy/caddy/Caddyfile` and the `/opt/stacks` git repo.

## Policy

**No blind auto-updates, ever.** Every image is pinned to an exact tag (or digest). Updates happen deliberately on your schedule, after reading release notes. Watchtower-style "always pull latest" is explicitly banned — it's how a set-and-forget box breaks at 3 a.m. (the original Watchtower project was archived read-only in Dec 2025).

Awareness is handled by **Diun**, which watches every running container's image and posts to the ntfy topic `diun` when a new version appears. This is *awareness only*, never action. (Diun is documented as "live on the NAS" in the architecture design; the runbook lists its config at `configs/docker-stack/stacks/diun/`.)

---

## End-to-End Flow (Standard Path)

1. **Awareness** — Diun detects a new tag → pushes a notification to your phone via ntfy.

2. **Read the release notes** — Especially for breaking-change projects: Immich (majors), Postgres (majors change data paths), Caddy, the *arrs.

3. **Bump the pin in git** — Edit the compose file in `configs/docker-stack/stacks/<name>/compose.yaml` (or `configs/nas/<name>/` for NAS stacks), e.g. `miniflux/miniflux:2.3.1 → 2.3.2`. Update the header comment if the version is named there. **The repo is the source of truth — never bump only on the host.**

4. **Commit + publish** — Commit to `home-config`, run `scripts/docs/publish-deploy.sh`, and mirror the change into `/opt/stacks/<name>/compose.yaml` (commit that repo too).

5. **Apply on the host:**
   ```bash
   ssh mini "cd /opt/stacks/<name> && docker compose pull && docker compose up -d"
   # NAS stacks: Container Manager → project → Action → Clean & rebuild
   ```

6. **Verify** — Service answers, logs clean, no crash loop:
   ```bash
   ssh mini "cd /opt/stacks/<name> && docker compose ps && docker compose logs --tail 20"
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<name>.tabaska.us
   ```

7. **Wiki** — Regenerate service pages (the pin is on the page):
   ```bash
   python3 foss-setup/scripts/docs/gen-wiki-services.py && bash foss-setup/scripts/docs/build-wiki.sh
   ```

8. **Meta-check** — Confirm repo pin == running container:
   ```bash
   ssh mini 'docker inspect <container> --format "{{.Config.Image}}"'
   ```

---

## How Immich Differs

Immich has three additional constraints:

- **Version pinning via `.env`** — The NAS Immich stack pins via `IMMICH_VERSION` in its `.env` file (not inline in the compose). The compose uses `${IMMICH_VERSION:?...}` with no floating `release` fallback, so it refuses to start unpinned.

- **Coordinated DB/Redis bumps** — The Valkey (redis) and VectorChord (postgres) images are **digest-pinned** to match the exact Immich release. When bumping `IMMICH_VERSION`, you must re-verify those digests against the release's official docker-compose.yml (`https://github.com/immich-app/immich/releases/latest/download/docker-compose.yml`). Postgres major upgrades are NOT automatic.

- **ML version-sync across hosts** — The rig's `immich-ml` container (`/opt/stacks/immich-ml`) must have the same `IMMICH_VERSION` in its `.env` as the NAS. If the rig `-cuda` image tag drifts, the `rig-immich-ml-version-match` check warns, and ML falls back to the slower NAS OpenVINO container (or fails entirely).

- **Rollback risk** — DB-migrating apps like Immich may not roll back cleanly, which is why reading release notes (step 2) is non-negotiable for Immich majors.

---

## How Caddy Differs

Caddy is **not a pulled image** — it's a **custom-built image** via `xcaddy` with the `caddy-dns/cloudflare` DNS module (required for the `local_tls` snippet's DNS-01 wildcard cert issuance). The stock Caddy image would fail to parse the `dns cloudflare` directive and the proxy would never start.

To update Caddy:
1. Bump the base version in `stacks/caddy/Dockerfile` (e.g. the `caddy:2.11.4` FROM line).
2. **Build** rather than pull: `docker compose build` (not just `docker compose pull`).
3. Then `docker compose up -d`.

The compose file must keep `build: .` (not a stock `image:` line). The `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` in the Caddy `.env` is required for ACME cert issuance via Cloudflare DNS-01.

---

## Rollback

The previous pin is one `git revert` away; `docker compose up -d` with the old tag restores the container. For DB-migrating apps (Immich), this is the critical reason step 2 (read release notes) exists — major DB changes may not be reversible.

For Caddy specifically, reverting the Dockerfile base version and rebuilding gives you the previous xcaddy binary.

**Claims to correct:**

I omitted the `foss-setup/` prefix. This is a real path difference — the script lives under `foss-setup/scripts/`, not at the repo root. **Corrected.**

3. **"NAS runs DSM (its own log rotation) and is excluded"** — The runbook says "The NAS runs DSM (its own log rotation) and is excluded." **Grounded.**

---

## UPS status: **No UPS is attached to the fleet.** UPS-triggered clean shutdown is not in place.

This is an accepted state, folded into the deferred tracker item **glue-01** ("UPS/NUT power resilience — no budget for a UPS right now").

---

## What the NUT config on mini was

The Mac mini had been configured as a NUT **netclient** (`nut-monitor` / `upsmon`) that monitored a UPS supposedly attached to the Synology NAS over TCP 3493:

```
UPS --USB--> DS920+ (DSM = NUT server)  <--net 3493--  mini (upsmon netclient)
```

The topology made sense on paper — the NAS is the most critical always-on box and has a USB port for a UPS. But **no UPS hardware was ever physically connected** to the NAS.

---

## What damage it caused

Because the NAS end never existed at runtime:

- **No UPS hardware** on the NAS — no `/dev/ups*`, no `/sys/class/power_supply/`, only Synology's internal boot device on USB.
- **DSM UPS support was OFF** (`SYNO.Core.ExternalDevice.UPS` → `enable=false`, `ACL_enable=false`, empty permitted-DiskStation list), so `upsd` never starts and port 3493 refuses connections.

So mini's `upsmon` retried every ~5 seconds **for 7+ days** — approximately **120,000 "Connection refused" errors** — filling the persistent journal to **4.1 G** while providing **zero** power-loss protection.

Liveness looked fine (the systemd unit was `active`); the consumer end (a reachable UPS) never existed. It was a textbook false-positive liveness trap.

---

## What was done about it (fix-31)

Operator decision: **retire the dead client** (no UPS budget now), and cap the journal so no chatty service can eat the disk again.

1. **Retired `nut-monitor` on mini** — stop + disable + **mask** the unit, set `MODE=none` in `/etc/nut/nut.conf`, and comment the managed `MONITOR` block in `/etc/nut/upsmon.conf`. A **masked** unit cannot be started by a dependency, an accidental `systemctl start`, or a stray re-run — the every-5s spam cannot recur.
2. **Guarded the setup script** — `scripts/setup/nut-client-ubuntu.sh` now refuses to run unless `NUT_REENABLE=1` is set, so re-provisioning cannot silently revive the doomed client.
3. **Capped journald on mini + rig** — `SystemMaxUse=1G`, `SystemMaxFileSize=128M`, applied by `apply-journald-cap.sh`, which also vacuumed existing bloat. mini's journal went **4.1 G → 1.0 G**. The NAS runs DSM (its own log rotation) and is excluded.
4. **Added verification checks** — `verification/checks.d/power-journal.yaml` asserts the unit stays masked/inactive and the journal isn't bloated. Failures page the `verification` ntfy topic.

---

## If you bought a UPS for the NAS tomorrow

The process is fully reversible and documented in the runbook:

### Step 1 — On the NAS (DSM)
1. **Control Panel → Hardware & Power → UPS** → enable UPS support (USB UPS) **and** "Enable network UPS server"
2. Add mini's IP `192.168.10.2` to "Permitted DiskStation Devices"
3. Confirm `upsd` is listening:
   ```
   ssh nas 'ss -ltn | grep 3493'
   ```

### Step 2 — On mini
Re-run the (now guarded) setup script:
```
sudo NUT_REENABLE=1 NAS_IP=192.168.10.4 foss-setup/scripts/setup/nut-client-ubuntu.sh
```
This unmasks the unit, restores `MODE=netclient`, and rewrites the `MONITOR` block.

### Step 3 — Verify end-to-end
```
upsc ups@192.168.10.4
```
Should return battery/status data. Then update `verification/checks.d/power-journal.yaml` (replace the `nut-monitor-retired` check with a reachability/consumer check) and re-run `deploy.sh`.

---

**TL;DR:** The NUT config on mini was a ghost client — it pointed at a UPS that never existed, causing 120k connection-refused errors and a 4.1 G journal over 7 days for zero protection. It's been retired (masked, journal-capped, guarded). If you buy a UPS tomorrow, the re-enable path is one DSM config toggle + one guarded script on mini.

## What's publicly reachable on your WAN IP

**Exactly one TCP port is open to the public internet: `32400 → NAS Plex`** (manual port-forward on the Dream Wall). This is the only intentional WAN exposure — an operator decision from 2026-07-17 so household users can stream over the internet without Tailscale.

Ports 80/443 (Caddy) are **not** reachable from the public internet: the UniFi firewall model is **allow Trusted → Untrusted; block Untrusted → Trusted** with narrow pinholes only, and no pinhole exists for 80/443. The gateway offers **no UPnP IGD or NAT-PMP** (verified with `upnpc`/`natpmpc` from the mini), so no LAN device can silently open additional ports. Everything else — every other service port — is unreachable from WAN.

The exposed Plex `/identity` endpoint is reachable from the internet by design (unauthenticated version + machine ID disclosure); everything else on Plex is token-gated.

## What should exist in public DNS for tabaska.us

The Cloudflare zone for `tabaska.us` should contain **zero A/AAAA host records**. The only records that should exist are:

| Type | Name | Value | Purpose |
|------|------|-------|---------|
| NS | `tabaska.us` | `courtney.ns.cloudflare.com`, `ryan.ns.cloudflare.com` | Delegation (nameservers moved from Squarespace/Google Cloud DNS) |
| MX | `tabaska.us` | `mail.protonmail.ch` (pri 10), `mailsec.protonmail.ch` (pri 20) | Proton Mail delivery (DNS-only / grey-cloud) |
| TXT | `tabaska.us` | `v=spf1 include:_spf.protonmail.ch mx ~all` | SPF |
| TXT | `tabaska.us` | `protonmail-verification=<exact value from current zone>` | Proton domain verification |
| NS | `minecraft.tabaska.us` | `ns1`/`ns2.playit-dns.com` | Game-server tunnel (playit.gg) |
| NS | `palworld.tabaska.us` | `ns1`/`ns2.playit-dns.com` | Game-server tunnel |
| NS | `bedrock.tabaska.us` | `ns1`/`ns2.playit-dns.com` | Game-server tunnel |

**`www.tabaska.us` must NOT exist in public DNS.** It was present at cutover time (pointing at `192.168.10.2`) but was deleted from Cloudflare on 2026-07-17 as the RFC1918 leak regression L53. Every other `*.tabaska.us` service name (plex, wiki, searxng, etc.) must return **NXDOMAIN** publicly — they resolve to `192.168.10.2` only via the AdGuard split-horizon rewrites on the LAN (both AdGuard instances carry `*.tabaska.us → 192.168.10.2`; the public Cloudflare zone does not carry a wildcard).

## How you'd notice if something extra got opened or published

There are **6 automated verification checks** in `foss-setup/verification/checks.d/edge.yaml` that continuously guard the public exposure posture. They run hourly/daily and page via ntfy:

### WAN port sweep (`edge-wan-port-posture`, crit)
A seedbox-side port scan (true off-net vantage — LAN-side probes only test NAT hairpin) hits 22 ports on your WAN IP. It expects **only 32400** to respond. Any other open port triggers a critical alert with the exact port numbers.

```bash
# The check runs from the seedbox:
for p in 22 80 443 853 2222 3000 3254 5000 5001 5945 6969 7878 8123 8443 8686 8787 8789 8790 8989 9696 13091 32400; do
  (timeout 4 bash -c "</dev/tcp/$WAN/$p" >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo $p) &
done; wait
# Anything besides 32400 = UNEXPECTED_OPEN:<ports>
```

### Plex identity check (`edge-plex-remote-identity`, warn)
Verifies that the service answering on port 32400 is actually your NAS Plex (pinned `machineIdentifier="70ffcfbb5dc9389e315070cf3a8af99c5fb340b4"`). If something else answers, you'd get an alert — a different host behind the forward would be a serious incident.

### Plex version staleness (`edge-plex-version-current`, warn)
Compares the exposed Plex build against the latest Synology DSM 7.2.2+ release from plex.tv. Warns if the exposed build is >14 days behind (unpatched-CVE risk on your one open port).

### Plex manual-port-mapping drift (`edge-plex-manual-port-mapping`, warn)
Checks that Plex's `ManualPortMappingMode` pref is `1` (manual) with `ManualPortMappingPort=32400`. If it drifts to auto/UPnP, the check fires — though the gateway has no UPnP, so this is a defensive guard against a Plex config revert.

### Cloudflare zone audit (`edge-public-dns-no-rfc1918`, warn)
Queries the Cloudflare API (using the token from `/etc/verification/env`) and scans all A/AAAA records in the `tabaska.us` zone. Fails if **any** record points at a private (RFC1918) IP. This catches the `www → 192.168.10.2` leak pattern and any future accidental private-IP records.

### www.tabaska.us NXDOMAIN check (`edge-public-dns-www-nxdomain`, warn)
Does a public `dig @1.1.1.1 www.tabaska.us A` and expects NXDOMAIN. If `www` reappears in public DNS, this fires.

---

**Summary:** One port (32400/Plex) open to the internet, zero A/AAAA host records in public DNS (only mail MX/TXT + game NS delegations), and 6 automated checks scanning from an off-net seedbox vantage plus the Cloudflare API that would alert on any unauthorized exposure within an hour.

## The off-mini dead-man: what pages you when the mini dies

### What it is

A systemd timer on the **rig** (`mini-deadman.timer` → `/usr/local/bin/mini-deadman.sh`), with canonical source at `configs/host/rig/mini-deadman/`. It is the **only** alerting mechanism that does not depend on the mini being alive.

### How it works

| Step | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Where it runs** | The **rig** (CachyOS + 3090 Ti, 24/7, off-mini). Unit: `mini-deadman.timer`. | alerting.md |
| **What it probes** | Every 5 minutes it does a **TCP probe** against mini's Caddy TLS edge at `192.168.10.2:443`. | alerting.md |
| **Threshold** | **Three consecutive misses** (~15 minutes) triggers a page. This window tolerates a Caddy restart. | alerting.md |
| **Delivery path** | On trigger it publishes a **max-priority message directly to the public `ntfy.sh`** server on a secret topic (vault `alerting.mini_deadman_ntfy_topic`), **bypassing mini entirely**. It re-pages **hourly** while down, and sends a `RECOVERED` notice when the edge returns. | alerting.md |
| **DNS independence** | The script resolves `ntfy.sh` against a public resolver (not mini's AdGuard), so DNS on mini being dead doesn't block the out-of-band path. | alerting.md |

### Why this delivery path was judged acceptable

The fleet leans no-cloud (foss-03), but a dead-man is only meaningful *outside* the thing it watches — and iOS push for the self-hosted ntfy already relays through ntfy.sh anyway. So for this **one safety-critical last resort** the fleet accepts a single public ntfy.sh relay carrying a bare alert (no secrets; the topic name is the read secret).

It was chosen over an external hosted heartbeat because a robust self-hosted off-mini watcher already exists (the rig) and needs no external account.

### Residual gap

If the **rig is also down** (whole-house power loss) there is no page — but that is self-evident, and the phone is on cellular. Optional belt-and-suspenders: a free healthchecks.io check pinged *by* mini (needs operator signup) — left as a documented follow-up.

### Self-test command (proves the path without mini)

```bash
ssh rig 'sudo MINI_DEADMAN_FORCE_DOWN=1 FAIL_THRESHOLD=1 \
  MINI_DEADMAN_STATE_DIR=/tmp/md-test /usr/local/bin/mini-deadman.sh'
# read it back off the public relay (topic from vault):
curl -s "https://ntfy.sh/<topic>/json?poll=1&since=5m"
```

Verified 2026-08-03: the forced-down run published *MINI DOWN — self-hosted alerting is dark* to ntfy.sh and it was read back off ntfy.sh — a path that never touched mini.

### Operator setup required

Subscribe the phone's ntfy app to the **ntfy.sh** server (not the self-hosted one) on the `alerting.mini_deadman_ntfy_topic` topic, with a loud/critical sound. This topic only ever fires when mini is dead.
